cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Today we use observations to measure material properties rather than just
substitute a value supplied by a textbook.
Start with a wire under tension.
Measure its original length and diameter, then observe the extension caused by
a known additional load.
A reference wire in a comparison arrangement helps reduce changes due to
support motion and common temperature effects.
An initial preload can straighten small kinks; use a consistent baseline for
the added force and added extension.
Young's modulus is stress divided by strain.
Stress is force divided by cross sectional area, and strain is extension
divided by original length.
Therefore Y equals F L divided by pi r squared times extension.
Our original example has length two meters, radius zero point five
millimeters,
added force twenty newtons, and added extension zero point two five
millimeters.
Convert both millimeter values to meters before calculating.
The result is about two point zero four times ten to the eleven pascals.
Notice that the force is already given in newtons; do not multiply it by g
again.
With several loads, plot force vertically against extension horizontally.
The elastic straight line slope is Y A divided by L, so Y is slope times L
over
area.
Add and remove loads gently, stay within the elastic limit, and look for
consistent return readings.
Diameter matters twice in the area, making its fractional measurement error
especially influential.
A smooth graph cannot rescue an incorrectly measured radius.
A narrow clean tube can make water rise above the surrounding surface.
At equilibrium, the upward vertical component of surface tension force
balances
the weight of the raised liquid in the simple model.
The contact line has circumference two pi r, giving upward force two pi r
gamma
cosine theta.
The liquid column weight is approximately pi r squared h rho g.
Cancel the common factors and solve: gamma equals rho g h r divided by twice
cosine theta.
For clean water wetting glass, theta is small and cosine theta is
approximately
one.
Measure the rise vertically from the outside liquid level to the meniscus
reference, and use the internal tube radius.
Our original example uses density one thousand kilograms per cubic meter, g
equal to nine point eight, rise three centimeters, and radius zero point five
millimeters.
With the small contact angle approximation, gamma is zero point zero seven
three five newtons per meter.
This estimate neglects the small meniscus volume correction; precise work can
require it.
The tube must be clean and vertical, and the radius must be measured reliably.
Now add a small amount of detergent in a controlled comparison.
Detergent usually reduces surface tension and can reduce capillary rise if
radius, density, temperature, and contact angle effects are sufficiently
controlled.
Do not attribute every height change solely to surface tension when wetting
conditions also change.
Pause before calculating: a stated diameter is twice the radius.
Using it unchanged would double the inferred surface tension in this formula.
Let's drop a small sphere through a viscous liquid.
Initially it accelerates, so the early falling speed is not automatically
terminal speed.
After drag grows enough, weight balances buoyancy plus viscous drag, and the
speed becomes approximately constant.
Time the motion between marks below the initial acceleration region.
For a sphere in creeping flow, Stokes drag is six pi eta r v.
Combining it with the weight and buoyancy gives eta equal to two r squared
times the sphere minus liquid density difference times g, divided by nine
terminal speed.
Our original data use radius zero point five millimeters, sphere density seven
thousand eight hundred, and liquid density one thousand two hundred sixty
kilograms per cubic meter.
The sphere covers twelve centimeters in sixty seconds at constant speed, so v
is zero point zero zero two meters per second.
With g equal to nine point eight, viscosity is about one point seven eight
pascal seconds.
It is not an acceleration and not measured in pascals alone.
Check that equal distances take approximately equal times in the timed region.
Use a container much wider than the sphere, avoid the walls, and record
temperature because viscosity is temperature dependent.
Stokes' formula assumes slow, low Reynolds number flow; it is not a universal
drag law for any fast object.
For multiple sphere sizes under the same valid conditions, terminal speed
plotted against radius squared should be approximately linear.
A size dependent deviation can signal that the assumptions or wall corrections
need attention.
Calorimetry asks where the thermal energy goes.
A hot solid is transferred into cooler water in an insulated calorimeter.
The solid loses energy, while both the water and the calorimeter gain energy.
If heat exchange with the surroundings is negligible, these changes balance.
Write hot solid mass times its specific heat times its temperature fall.
Set that equal to water heat capacity plus calorimeter heat capacity, all
multiplied by their temperature rise.
The calorimeter is not magically thermally invisible.
Our original example has a zero point one kilogram solid initially at one
hundred degrees Celsius.
Water mass is zero point two kilograms at twenty degrees.
Its specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram kelvin.
The calorimeter's effective heat capacity is twenty joules per kelvin, and the
final temperature is twenty four degrees.
Water and container together gain three thousand four hundred forty joules.
Divide by zero point one times the solid's seventy six degree temperature
fall.
The solid's inferred specific heat is about four hundred fifty three joules
per
kilogram kelvin.
Temperature differences in Celsius and kelvin have the same numerical size.
In a real supervised experiment, measure the hot solid's temperature, transfer
promptly, minimize carried hot water, and stir gently for a uniform reading.
If the liquid's specific heat is unknown instead, use a solid of known heat
capacity and solve the same balance for the liquid.
Never leave both specific heats unknown with only one balance equation.
These ideal calculations do not remove heat loss uncertainty from actual
observations.
Let's finish with the skill that links every experiment: making an honest
inference from imperfect data.
Repeat readings to reveal scatter, use their mean when appropriate, and apply
calibration or zero corrections consistently.
A fixed zero error does not disappear just because you measured ten times.
That is the difference between reducing random variation and correcting a
systematic offset.
Graphs help reveal relationships and unusual points.
Label each axis with the measured quantity and unit, choose a useful scale,
and
fit a trend to the data rather than joining every point with a jagged line.
For a straight relationship, calculate slope using well separated points on
the
fitted line.
Do not automatically force a line through the origin unless the physical model
and corrected observations justify it.
Here is a JEE error example.
Young's modulus depends on inverse radius squared.
If radius has a small two percent error and the other contributions are
negligible, its contribution to the maximum fractional error in Y is
approximately four percent.
The same inverse square dependence holds when the diameter is used
consistently
in area.
A conservative maximum error sum uses absolute fractional contributions; an
independent statistical uncertainty calculation can use a different
combination
rule.
State which kind of error estimate you are making.
Before accepting a result, check dimensions, radius versus diameter,
temperature, and whether the experiment met its assumptions.
A neat numerical answer is useful only when the measurement model is
justified.
Our worked data are original classroom examples, not claims that we performed
these experiments or reproduced an official exam question.
